extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing creative writers (fiction and narrative nonfiction) seeking craft and mindset guidance
extracted.subtask_description: A concise set of creative-writing craft rules and writerly mindset principles drawn from Annie Dillard's The Writing Life, aimed at guiding sentence-level practice, project choices, work habits, and how to approach revision and persistence on long works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kill your darlings
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to remove even the best-written passages if they do not serve the work's form or cohesion. Dillard: 'The part you must jettison is not only the best-written part; it is also, oddly, that part which was to have been the very point.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat cherished passages as possible sacrifices as the book's form hardens; assess whether a passage is essential to the final structure even if it was the impetus for writing. Use the 'does this serve the whole?' test rather than sentimental attachment. Example/illustration: Henry James' observation about surrendering the thing one meant to keep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every word should matter / write with urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: Write with the economy and urgency of someone who 'writes as if you were dying' — ask what you would write if your time were short and ensure each word counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume an audience of 'terminal patients' and avoid trivialities; prioritize urgent, meaningful material. The post echoes Dillard's prompt: 'Every word should matter. Ask yourself: what would you write if you knew your time was short?' Use this to focus subject choice and eliminate filler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer's block signals deeper issues
rubrics_metrics.description: View writer's block not as mere laziness but as a signal of structural laws in existing writing or shortcomings in what the writer hopes to add: something about the work (or the writer's approach) is preventing progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the block ('you cannot do nothing') and diagnose whether the blockage is due to form, structure, or lack of clarity about contribution; take deliberate action rather than waiting it out. Dillard's 'worker will not go' analogy stresses recognizing the problem and responding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow long timeframes — writing takes years
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that serious books typically take years to write ('It takes years to write a book—between two and ten years') and that rapid examples are statistical outliers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic expectations for project timelines; value accumulation of inventions, reading, and experience over time. Use examples (Faulkner's anomalous rapid work) to remind writers not to measure their process by extreme outliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't write to entertain non-readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Write for readers who want literature rather than trying to craft books aimed at people who don't read; Dillard warns against struggling to appeal to non-readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on what books uniquely offer rather than trying to imitate mass-entertainment media; understand and accept the likely audience for literary work rather than compromising voice and depth to chase non-reader attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study literature and deliberate reading choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer 'studies literature, not the world' — be careful about what you read and learn because that reading will shape what you write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose reading models and influences intentionally; study great writers and the works that trained other successful authors (examples given: Hemingway studied Hamsun and Turgenev, Faulkner's debts, Thoreau loved Homer, etc.). Use those models to develop craft rather than relying solely on lived experience or trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer unappealing, distraction-free workspaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a workspace with minimal visual distraction—'a room with no view'—so imagination can meet memory in the dark; avoid appealing workplaces that invite distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position desk against a blank wall, choose simple or even austere rooms (Dillard's examples: cinder-block cell over a parking lot, pine shed under trees) to minimize temptation and external stimulation. The environment should support concentration and inward attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love sentences — cultivate sentence-level attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Enjoy and care about sentences themselves; a key test of readiness to be a writer is whether you 'like sentences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize sentence craft as a fundamental ingredient of good writing; if you do not care for sentences, begin by practicing and appreciating sentence-level work (sound, rhythm, precision) before attempting larger projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer long, ambitious projects over many short pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Dillard argues it 'makes more sense to write one big book' because long projects accumulate years' inventions and reading, allowing a writer to pour all they possess into a single ambitious work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider devoting energy to a single sustained project (novel or long nonfiction) rather than dispersing effort across many short stories or essays; recognize that sentence difficulty exists in any subject, so place effort where it yields the deepest payoff over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your best material now — don't hoard
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't save your best lines or discoveries for later; 'spend it all, shoot it, play it, lose it, all, right away, every time' — hoarding what seems good is destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you find something good, put it into the work immediately rather than banking it for a later place; the impulse to save signals you should spend now because more material will arise later. Avoid secrecy about learned material; generosity in giving it away prevents loss (the 'open your safe and find ashes' image).
